source.title: The effect of root hairs on root water uptake is determined by root–soil contact and root hair shrinkage
source.license: Creative Commons Attribution License (explicitly stated on page 1 of the accessible original PDF; version not asserted)
source.article_type: Original research; synchrotron imaging and image-based water-flow modeling

claims.claim: Maize plants were grown for 14 days in loamy soil and root–soil geometries were obtained by synchrotron X-ray CT; water simulations were not intended to reproduce the water state during scanning.
claims.location: Materials and Methods, opening paragraphs; Plant growth; Imaging and image processing
claims.evidence_type: Experimental method and stated modeling scope

claims.claim: The model used six static root segments approximately 1.4 mm long and compared each imaged geometry before and after digital removal of hairs.
claims.location: Materials and Methods → Mathematical model; Statistics; Figures 2 and 5

claims.claim: The outer soil water potential was varied while the inner root outlet boundary was fixed at −1.5 MPa; steady-state solutions were compared.
claims.location: Mathematical model, equations 3–6; Results, opening paragraphs

claims.claim: In the driest main scenario (outer potential −1.26 MPa), hairs increased simulated water uptake by 24 ± 18% across the six samples before accounting for shrinkage.
claims.location: Results, paragraph beginning “Our model revealed...”; Figure 8a
claims.evidence_type: Simulated result; not measured field uptake

claims.claim: Hair-induced increase in root–soil contact explained 86% of the variance in the modeled uptake benefit (R²=0.865, P=0.007), not 86% of total water uptake.
Early-shrinkage scenario 2 eliminated the modeled positive hair effect; later-shrinkage scenario 1 retained benefit approximately from −1 to −0.1 MPa.
claims.location: Results, shrinkage paragraphs; Figures 4 and 8b; Table 2
claims.evidence_type: Two parameterized shrinkage scenarios, assessed on the sample with greatest initial hair benefit

claims.claim: The model shows steeper local matric-potential gradients near the hairless root, whereas hairs distribute uptake over a wider radial region.
claims.location: Results; Figures 6–7; Discussion, first mechanistic paragraphs

claims.claim: The authors state the model is not intended for entire root systems and discuss container artifacts, ignored structure modification, and uncertainty in root-hair conductivity.
claims.location: Discussion, paragraphs beginning “We would like to emphasise...”, “Limitations of our model...”, “We are aware...”, and “Another limitation...”

claims.claim: Root hydraulic parameterization drew on water-flux work on lupin roots, and root hair cell-wall conductivity was not represented explicitly.
claims.location: Materials and Methods → Parameterisation; Discussion → limitation of root-hair hydraulic conductivity

limits: Six very short static maize segments from one loamy soil, not whole sorghum plants.
The quoted 24% benefit is a mean simulation difference under specific fixed boundaries without the additional shrinkage model.
The 86% result is a fitted relationship across six geometries and is not the water share taken up by hairs.
Shrinkage was assessed through two hydraulic scenarios on the sample with the largest initial hair effect.
Whole-system growth, new exploration of wet soil, dynamic shoot demand, and all soil-structure changes were not included.
Hair hydraulic parameterization and container-scale geometry introduce uncertainty.
inference_for_user: The mechanism suggests testing soil-contact and drying-dependent conductance descriptions in a sorghum CPlantBox/DuMuX workflow; parameter values and whole-plant outcomes require sorghum-relevant data and independent validation.
copyright_basis: Original PDF page 1 states Creative Commons Attribution License; all lesson prose is newly written.
